opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I'd break it into a few layers.

First, there's raw reasoning and instruction following. Can the model take a high-level goal like "build a shelter before nightfall," decompose it into sub-goals, and adapt when something goes wrong? The open Llama models have gotten good at this. For a lot of high-level planning in game worlds, they're already capable enough, especially when you give them a good prompt structure and some memory scaffolding.

Second, and this is where it gets harder, is grounding. A game world isn't just text. The agent has to perceive the environment, understand spatial relationships, track state over long horizons, and turn plans into low-level actions. Language models alone aren't natively good at that. In our earlier work on Voyager in Minecraft, the trick was to use code as the action space. The model writes programs that call the game's APIs, so you're using what LLMs are best at, which is writing code, and you keep a growing skill library the agent can reuse. That's a strong pattern, and it works reasonably well with capable open models, though the frontier models were still noticeably better at writing correct, composable code on the first try.

Third is the self-improvement loop. Can the model look at execution errors and environment feedback, critique its own behavior, and fix it? That reflective capability scales with model quality. Smaller models tend to get stuck in loops or hallucinate fixes that don't address the real problem.

So how do I actually assess it? I put the model in an open-ended world and measure things like how many distinct skills it discovers, how fast it climbs a tech tree, and whether it can generalize to a new world with novel tasks. Static benchmarks don't capture that. You need embodied, open-ended evaluation, because what matters is whether the agent keeps learning and exploring, not whether it answers one question correctly.

My overall take is that Llama models are a fantastic foundation, especially because they're open. You can fine-tune them on gameplay trajectories, distill from stronger models, and deploy them cheaply at scale, which matters if you want thousands of agents in a world at once. The gap to the frontier is real but shrinking. And the bigger long-term shift is moving from pure language models to multimodal foundation models that take in pixels and output actions directly. That's where I think game agents, and eventually robots, are heading.

r001.rationale: The response says open Llama models are already capable enough for much high-level planning and discusses measuring skill discovery, but it does not judge them insufficiently diverse.

r002.rationale: The response does not assess whether Llama agents produce sufficiently engaging behaviors or say their behaviors fall short.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because the gap between what a model can do in a chat window and what it can do when it's actually embodied in a world is enormous. The way I tend to frame it is: a game world is just a very forgiving simulator. The physics is simplified, the action space is discrete or close to it, and you get free reward signals from the game itself. So if a model can't drive an agent in Minecraft or a similar environment, it's definitely not going to drive a robot in your kitchen. Games are the easy exam before the hard exam.

Now, specifically on Llama. When we built Voyager, that was on GPT-4, and the thing that made it work wasn't raw knowledge about Minecraft, it was the ability to write code that acts as a skill, run it, read the error from the environment, and fix it. That loop. Self-verification, iterative refinement. So when I assess a new open model, the first question I ask isn't "does it know what diamonds are made of," it's "can it close that loop reliably over hundreds of steps without drifting." Because an agent is a long-horizon thing. A model that's right ninety-five percent of the time on a single call is a model that's wrong almost certainly over a fifty-step episode. The error compounds.

And what we've seen with the Llama generations is that they've been closing that gap faster than I expected. The 405B class models are genuinely in the neighborhood for a lot of the planning and code-writing pieces. Where they still fall off is in the messier parts. Grounding, meaning: here's a screenshot or a structured observation, what is actually happening right now, and did my last action do what I thought it did. Spatial reasoning. And honestly, knowing when they're stuck. A good agent has to recognize "I've tried this three times and it's not working, let me step back," and smaller models tend to loop.

The other thing I'd say is that the open weights matter enormously for this specific problem, more than for chat. Because with a game you can generate unlimited data. You can roll out the agent, you can get ground truth from the engine, and then you can fine-tune. You can't do that with a closed API. So even if a given Llama checkpoint is a bit behind frontier on day one, the fact that you can specialize it on millions of trajectories from your own world means it's often the better foundation for an agent in practice. The base model is the starting point, not the ceiling.

So my honest assessment is: capable enough to build real research prototypes today, and increasingly capable enough to ship things if you're willing to do the data work in the loop. Not capable enough yet to just drop in zero-shot and have a general-purpose agent that behaves well across arbitrary games. But I think that last part is a training-data problem more than an architecture problem, and games are exactly where we can manufacture that data.

r001.rationale: The response notes limits in grounding, spatial reasoning, and zero-shot performance, but does not judge Llama models insufficiently diverse in their game-world behaviors.

r002.rationale: The response does not assess whether Llama agents’ behaviors are engaging; its limitations concern reliability and generalization.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by powering an agent. If you mean taking raw pixels and producing precise actions in real time, that’s a very different challenge from deciding, “I should collect wood, make a tool, and build a shelter.” A Llama model might serve as the high-level planner, while a separate controller executes those actions.

So I would assess it in a closed loop inside the game. Can it accomplish a task? When an action fails, can it use the feedback to recover? Can it handle a new situation rather than repeat a familiar sequence? A plausible plan in text isn’t enough—you need to see whether the agent actually gets things done.

Without specifying the model, the game, and the tools it has access to, I wouldn’t give a blanket yes or no. The capability comes from the whole system, and the test is how reliably that system behaves over time.

r001.rationale: The response gives no judgment that current Llama models are insufficiently diverse; it says capability depends on the model, game, tools, and whole system.

r002.rationale: The response does not assess whether the behaviors are engaging and gives no judgment that current Llama models are insufficient in that respect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to evaluate them inside the game loop. A model can give a very convincing explanation of what it wants to do, but can it actually execute a plan, observe what happened, and recover when something goes wrong? That’s a much higher bar than answering a question.

For Llama, I’d separate the underlying model from the system around it. What observations does it receive? What actions can it take? Does it have memory, tools, or a library of skills? If every action is a low-level button press, the problem is very hard. If it can invoke something like “navigate to this location,” then it can spend more of its capacity on planning.

So I’d test it on progressively longer tasks, with unfamiliar environments and real opportunities to fail. Can it complete the task reliably? Can it adapt when the environment changes? How much human scaffolding does it need? That tells you much more about whether it can power an agent than how fluent its dialogue sounds.

r001.rationale: The response proposes testing execution, recovery, adaptation, and scaffolding, but does not judge whether current Llama models produce sufficiently diverse behaviors.

r002.rationale: The response says fluent dialogue is not enough, but does not judge whether current Llama models produce sufficiently engaging behaviors.
